source: Cai et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Tool Makers (LATM), ICLR 2024
finding: A strong model writes a reusable Python tool once; a cheap model then uses it. Tool-making and tool-using are split into maker and user.
numbers: Six tasks. GPT-3.5 Turbo as user, CoT vs LATM: Logical Deduction 66.4 vs 79.7; Tracking Objects 61.6 vs 99.6; Dyck 20.4 vs 92.2; Word Sorting 59.2 vs 98.3; Chinese Remainder 0.0 vs 100.0; Schedule Meeting 18.9 vs 100.0. GPT-4 was the maker.
limits: Well-defined function-style tasks. GPT-4 call cost C is over 15x the GPT-3.5 call cost c.
agent_relevance: Direct fit for a library of helper tools: pay for the strong model once, reuse cheaply.

source: Cai et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Tool Makers (LATM), ICLR 2024
finding: With the tool, the cheap user matches or beats the strong model using CoT. On Dyck, GPT-3.5 as user beat GPT-4 as user, because GPT-4 rewrote the argument before calling the tool.
numbers: GPT-4 user, CoT vs LATM: Logical 88.8 vs 86.6; Tracking 100 vs 100; Dyck 63.6 vs 87.5; Word Sort 90.9 vs 99.1; CRT 0.0 vs 100.0; Schedule 55.6 vs 100.0. Cost O(nc+C) vs O(nC).
limits: A stronger user can over-process the input and damage the tool call.
agent_relevance: Pass raw input to the tool. Do not let the model pre-edit arguments; let code make the call.

source: Cai et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Tool Makers (LATM), ICLR 2024
finding: The dispatcher step (cache lookup) was accurate: finding the right existing tool and deciding when a new tool is needed.
numbers: Tool identification 95% +/- 2% on 100 mixed samples (5 random test sets). Deciding to request tool-making for an unseen task: 96% +/- 3%.
limits: GPT-3.5 Turbo dispatcher; six tasks only.
agent_relevance: A router that decides reuse vs build can be a cheap slot behind a code-checked gate.

source: Cai et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Tool Makers (LATM), ICLR 2024
finding: Weak models fail at making tools, because the tool only works on the training samples and does not generalise.
numbers: GPT-3.5 Turbo as tool maker failed all 5 trials on Logical Deduction and Tracking Shuffled Objects. It worked on easy tasks such as Word Sorting.
limits: Maker capacity matters most on hard tasks. Tool validated on only 3 validation samples.
agent_relevance: Supports G3: validate a new tool on held-out cases, not on the cases it was written from.

source: Yuan et al. (2024) CRAFT: Customizing LLMs by Creating and Retrieving from Specialized Toolsets, ICLR 2024
finding: Build a task-specific toolset offline: GPT-4 solves training examples, solutions are validated, abstracted into reusable snippets and deduplicated. At test time the model retrieves tools.
numbers: Average 43.16% relative F1 improvement over the best baseline across VQA, tabular and math tasks. Toolset construction cost about 2,500 USD in total. Backbone GPT-3.5-Turbo.
limits: Needs GPT-4 plus training examples. Cost is up front.
agent_relevance: The validate, abstract, dedupe pipeline is what an agent library needs.

source: Yuan et al. (2024) CRAFT: Customizing LLMs by Creating and Retrieving from Specialized Toolsets, ICLR 2024
finding: Generic library tools (NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, SymPy) did not help and sometimes hurt. Relevance of the tool matters more than count.
numbers: Authors: external library tools fail to improve performance and may hurt (e.g. mathematical reasoning). CodeLlama backbones near-random in this setting.
limits: Stated in text; open models weak at tool use in 2023.
agent_relevance: Curated, task-fitted tools beat big generic toolboxes. Keep the library small and relevant.

source: Yuan et al. (2024) CRAFT: Customizing LLMs by Creating and Retrieving from Specialized Toolsets, ICLR 2024
finding: Ablations show abstraction and multi-view retrieval both matter. Matching on problem, function name and docstring together beats BM25 or SimCSE on tool names alone.
numbers: Removing the name view dropped one score to 37.1 (w/o Name) and the docstring view to 42.4 (w/o Docstring) in Table 3; abstraction removal gave a clear drop; more tools gave steady soft-accuracy gains.
limits: Single backbone. Full-model comparison row not cleanly parsed from the PDF.
agent_relevance: Tool descriptions (name plus docstring) drive retrieval. Write them to a standard.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
finding: Voyager keeps a growing library of verified executable skills in Minecraft, with an automatic curriculum and self-verification. It climbs a tool ladder: wooden, stone, iron, diamond.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations, 3.3x more than baselines. Tech tree: wooden 15.3x faster, stone 8.5x, iron 6.4x; only agent to reach diamond. Travelled 2.3x longer distances.
limits: Minecraft only; GPT-4; baselines AutoGPT, ReAct, Reflexion.
agent_relevance: Best-known skill-library agent. The tool ladder, each tool built from earlier ones, is the stepped tool analogue.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
finding: Ablations show which parts carry the result. The skill library stops late plateaus; self-verification is the most important feedback type.
numbers: Random curriculum: discovered items drop 93%. No self-verification: drop 73%. GPT-4 gets 5.7x more unique items than GPT-3.5 for code. No skill library: progress plateaus in later stages.
limits: Numbers read from text; figure not parsed.
agent_relevance: Skills help only when a verify step admits them (G2, G3). Order of tasks matters.

source: Tian et al. (2025) MacGyver: Are Large Language Models Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: Dataset of 1,600+ problems needing unconventional use of objects (functional fixedness). Humans and LLMs fail in different ways.
numbers: Over 82% of solvable problems need unconventional tool use. About 78% solvable, 22% unsolvable. GPT-4: 18.9% efficient solutions, 37.5% infeasible. Majority-human correct 79.3% vs GPT-4 73.3%.
limits: Text only for both groups. Human panel size not extracted.
agent_relevance: Models over-propose and ignore physical limits. Humans are all-or-none; models are middling.

source: Tian et al. (2025) MacGyver: Are Large Language Models Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: Error analysis of 200 infeasible GPT-4 answers: most are wrong tool use; some use tools not in the inventory or ignore constraints.
numbers: Wrong tool usage 42.4%; not achieving goal 17.7%; unavailable tools 16.9%; wrong spatial understanding 10.8%; unfaithful to constraints 9.5%. (Mapping of two middle values from a messy table; may be swapped.)
limits: Manual review of 200 items, one model.
agent_relevance: An inventory and constraint check by code could catch about 26% (hallucinated tools plus ignored constraints).

source: Tian et al. (2025) MacGyver: Are Large Language Models Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: Two prompts changed results: iterative step-wise reflection and divergent-convergent thinking. Reflection helps only the strongest model.
numbers: GPT-4 on 180 solvable problems: reflection cut infeasible answers by 9.7 points, div-conv by 4.3. Div-conv raised efficient answers by 6.5 points, reflection by 2.2. Claude2 and Llama2-13b gained nothing from reflection; div-conv helped all three.
limits: Single-digit gains; 180 problems; reflection is model-judged, which conflicts with the schema rule against self-grading.
agent_relevance: Divergent-then-convergent is safer. Self-reflection needs a code or environment check.

source: Yiu, Kosoy and Gopnik (2023) Imitation versus Innovation: What children can do that large language and language-and-vision models cannot (yet)?
finding: Tool innovation task: pick a non-obvious object with the right function (plant pot to hold hot coffee) over a similar but useless one (coffee lid). Models did the association task well and the innovation task poorly.
numbers: Children 3-7 (n=42): imitation 88.4%, innovation 85.2%. Adults (n=30): imitation 84.9%, innovation 95.7%. Models (gpt-3.5-turbo, text-davinci-003, Claude, FLAN-T5-XXL, Bloomz) near human on imitation, much worse on innovation; they chose the coffee lid.
quote: models are almost as capable of identifying superficial commonalities between objects as humans are
limits: Model scores given only in words, no table. Early 2023 models; newer models may differ. Position paper, preliminary.
agent_relevance: Retrieving tools by association picks the nearest neighbour. Retrieve by function and constraint.

source: Wang et al. (2024) LLMs in the Imaginarium: Tool Learning through Simulated Trial and Error (STE)
finding: Existing LLMs use real APIs unreliably. The paper cites crow work (Emery and Clayton 2004) for trial and error, imagination and memory, and builds STE: imagine usage scenarios, try the API, reflect, store short- and long-term memory.
numbers: ToolBench, 50 APIs: GPT-4 with ICL 60.8% correctness; ToolLLaMA-v2 37.3%. STE lifts Mistral-Instruct-7B to 76.8% (+46.7 points), above GPT-4 with ICL.
limits: Fine-tuning on the 50 APIs. Continual learning needs rehearsal: vanilla fine-tuning forgets (1.7% vs 76.1% with rehearsal on an earlier batch).
agent_relevance: Cheap way to learn a tool before use: explore with executed feedback and keep notes.

source: Wang et al. (2024) LLMs in the Imaginarium: Tool Learning through Simulated Trial and Error (STE)
finding: Ablation: execution feedback, short-term memory, long-term memory and reflection are each needed.
numbers: Without long-term memory only 71.7% of trials concerned distinct subjects and attributes were skewed; with it all queries were distinct. No execution feedback gave ill-formed API calls.
limits: Diversity numbers from one case study (forecast_weather).
agent_relevance: A per-tool log of what was tried avoids repeating probes.

source: Wolflein et al. (2025) LLM Agents Making Agent Tools (ToolMaker)
finding: ToolMaker turns a paper plus GitHub repo into a working tool: install, plan, implement, closed-loop self-repair with tests.
numbers: 15 tasks, 100+ unit tests: ToolMaker 80% (12/15) vs OpenHands 20% (3/15). ToolMaker 21.8 actions and 0.94 USD per tool; OpenHands 7.5 actions and 0.15 USD.
limits: 15 tasks, mostly life science; one failure was a non-representative example call.
agent_relevance: Logged install commands and reset environments make repair reproducible. About 6x the cost for 4x the success.

source: Wolflein et al. (2025) LLM Agents Making Agent Tools (ToolMaker)
finding: Adding paper summaries did not raise success; it only cut repair iterations. OpenHands failed mostly at environment setup.
numbers: Nearly half of OpenHands environment definitions were invalid. One task needed 9 repair iterations (33 actions).
limits: Ablation on the same 15 tasks.
agent_relevance: The example invocation must be representative (G3: check a tool on something it was not fitted to).

source: Hsieh et al. (2023) Tool Documentation Enables Zero-Shot Tool-Usage with Large Language Models
finding: Tool documentation beats demonstrations. With docs, zero-shot matches few-shot; without docs, results depend on the number of demos.
numbers: With docs, 0-shot equals 16-shot on TabMWP and 12-shot on NLVRv2, and beats 10-shot demos on ScienceQA. On a new LLM-Cloud CLI set with hundreds of tools, docs-only zero-shot beat few-shot without docs.
limits: Six tasks; demos still help when docs are missing.
agent_relevance: Give every helper tool a standard doc entry (purpose, args, flags). Demos come second.

source: Hsieh et al. (2023) Tool Documentation Enables Zero-Shot Tool-Usage with Large Language Models
finding: Failure mode of demos: the model copies a familiar command and hallucinates flags. Docs fix this and reveal hidden steps.
numbers: Demos led to -P (from scp) instead of --port. The docs-only run used --port and the hidden step of creating a topic before sending messages.
limits: One worked example.
agent_relevance: Docs reduce prior-driven misuse of unfamiliar tools.

source: Schick et al. (2023) Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
finding: A 6.7B GPT-J model is fine-tuned on its own filtered API-call samples (calculator, QA, search, translation, calendar). A call is kept only if it lowers loss on later tokens.
numbers: Zero-shot, clearly beats the much larger GPT-3 175B on several tasks; on QA with Wikipedia search it beats same-size baselines but falls short of GPT-3 175B.
quote: achieves much stronger zero-shot results, clearly outperforming a much larger GPT-3 model
limits: Single-step calls only, no chaining, prompt-sensitive.
agent_relevance: Filter tool calls by a usefulness test, not the model's say-so.

source: Chen et al. (2026) SkillCraft: Can LLM Agents Learn to Use Tools Skillfully?
finding: Benchmark of 126 compositional tool tasks (63 easy, 42 medium, 21 hard). In Skill Mode the agent composes atomic tools into executable skills, verifies, caches and reuses them.
numbers: One model: success 109/126 (87%) to 114/126 (90%); tokens 1.23M to 0.26M (-79%); cost 1.77 to 0.43 USD (-75%). Up to 80% token cut. MiniMax-M2.1 saved only 11%.
limits: Open-weight models had under 90% overall and under 60% on hard tasks. Weak models follow the prompt without composing.
agent_relevance: A verified skill library saves cost, but only with a capable composer.

source: Chen et al. (2026) SkillCraft: Can LLM Agents Learn to Use Tools Skillfully?
finding: Hierarchical skills (skills calling skills) hurt: errors spread through the dependency tree.
numbers: Hierarchical mode lowers end-to-end success from 90% to 79% and weakens savings (0.26M vs 0.60M tokens).
limits: Single model in this comparison.
agent_relevance: Keep the library flat, or re-verify a skill when a dependency changes.

source: Klein-Seetharaman et al. (2026) Lomekwi: Resource-Bounded Tool Discovery in LLM Agents
finding: Separates tool use from tool discovery, as in animal work: curiosity (gather parts), recognition (realise a tool can be built), efficiency (use it). Recognition falls as models grow.
numbers: Qwen3.5 recognition 0.29 (2B), 0.10 (4B), 0.05 (9B), 0.02 (27B), while win rate rises 0.46 to 0.88. Tool calls per episode 3.1 to 0.2; episodes with no tool call 61/180 to 154/180; solved by hand 35 to 157 of 180. Claude Opus builds less than Haiku. Qwen3 peaks 0.93 at 8B then 0.06 at 32B.
limits: Preprint; game and long-division settings; models are not told a tool is needed; Claude size is only ordinal.
agent_relevance: Big models grind by hand instead of building. The trigger to build a tool must come from the program (budget, repeat count), not the model.

source: Klein-Seetharaman et al. (2026) Lomekwi: Resource-Bounded Tool Discovery in LLM Agents
finding: Maps the decomposition on to Voyager. Voyager works partly because its GPT-4 controller already knows the recipes, which hides the recognition term.
numbers: Cites Neldner et al. (2020): children use tools before they invent them. 10 models (3 Claude, 7 Qwen), 180 episodes per model.
limits: Argument is heuristic.
agent_relevance: Do not expect tool invention to appear unprompted; give it a state with a code trigger.

source: WebSearch summary: LLMs on the New Caledonian crow metatool paradigm
finding: A search for LLMs tested on the crow metatool (stick-to-stick) paradigm found no direct paper. Closest are the Yiu et al. innovation task and Lomekwi.
numbers: None found.
limits: Searches were limited (2 WebSearch calls; arXiv and OpenAlex APIs returned empty or errors). Absence is not proof.
agent_relevance: Direct crow-paradigm tests of LLMs look like an open gap.
